, which documents the identical ordering choice: the child’s state passed in is already updated by the time an ancestor sees the event. The event is always forwarded to the child; there’s no way to intercept or veto it, and none is needed.

That’s not a minor implementation detail — it’s what makes a parent reaction safe even when it goes on to destroy or replace the very child subtree the event came from (say, tearing a child down after too many failed attempts). Since the child already, safely, applied the event to itself before any ancestor gets a look, there’s never a moment where a stale event is still “in flight” toward a subtree an ancestor’s reaction just tore down. An earlier design that ran the parent’s reaction
before
forwarding had exactly that problem in the other direction: a real app’s login screen guarded
on
, where

same
event had already flipped to
moments earlier — rejecting every legitimate submit. Forwarding first, always, removes that entire class of bug rather than requiring each handler to remember to avoid it.

A lightweight library for managing state in iOS applications, designed with simplicity, testability, and scalability in mind.
Explore the core concepts of the Statostore pattern through examples.
Statoscope is a small library to build apps with state management,
testing, effects management and dependency injection.
